sections.label: THE PROBLEM
sections.heading: Do you treat a substance as a "mimic of psychosis", as something that "opens the mind", or as something that "produces delusion"?

items.text: The same substance, under three different names, creates three different expectations. In the 1950s scientists were wrestling with exactly this naming problem.

sections.label: SECTION 1 · ORIGIN
sections.heading: Osmond and Huxley: the birth of a word

items.def: A contest for a word

The pair sought a new word to describe the experience (1956 correspondence)
Huxley proposed: "phanerothyme" — to show the spirit
Osmond won: "psychedelic" — announced in 1957 at the New York Academy of Sciences
They settled it with a legendary rhyme (next slide)

lines: British-Canadian psychiatrist; researched schizophrenia with mescaline and LSD
In 1953 he guided the writer Aldous Huxley through a mescaline experience
Huxley's "The Doors of Perception" (1954) grew out of that experience
To fathom Hell or soar angelic,
just take a pinch of psychedelic.

items.def: Osmond's reply rhyme. Huxley's proposal was: "To make this mundane world sublime, take half a gram of phanerothyme." Osmond's more memorable line fixed the name.

sections.label: SECTION 1 · ETYMOLOGY
sections.heading: Let us take the word apart

items.def: mind · soul
The idea: the substance reveals what is already in the mind
Mind-revealing. Neutral-to-positive; the most common term in science and therapy.
"Generating the divine within". Emphasises ritual/spiritual context; preferred in traditional use.
Producing delusion/illusion. Medically neutral but criticised for implying "not real".

items.text: Three names for the same substance: the word you choose usually gives away your attitude towards it.

items.def: There is no single "psychedelic"

items.text: Shared signature: they stimulate the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor in the brain. They do not trigger the addictive "reward" circuits in the same way.

Natural, in mushrooms; converts to psilocin in the body. 4–6 hours. The most researched today.
On its own very short (minutes) but intense. Extended to hours with ayahuasca.
In peyote / San Pedro cacti. Long-lasting. Among the oldest known.
Does not radically alter perception; creates intense emotional closeness, trust and empathy. Softens the fear response → interest in trauma work. Known on the street as "ecstasy".
Separates consciousness from the body. A different system (glutamate/NMDA). An anaesthetic in medicine for decades; the only example legal and approved for depression.
Substances with their own profile, such as ibogaine (addiction research, but serious cardiac risks) and salvia (very short, potent, distinctive).
Very intense, brief
Durations are typical ranges; they vary by dose, person and setting. Legal status is covered in Sections 5–6.
Wrong. Different chemistry, different mechanism, different effect and legal status.
Wrong. Being natural does not mean risk-free (see Module 5).
This popular myth has no scientific basis; but real risks do exist.
True. The effect depends largely on the person and the setting (set & setting).

sections.label: CONTEXT
sections.heading: The ritual use of consciousness-altering plants and mushrooms reaches far back beyond written history.

items.text: This use was not for individual pleasure; it was in the context of healing, community and the sacred — the ancestor of modern therapy's idea of "set and setting".

items.def: Psilocybin mushrooms ("teonanácatl" — flesh of the gods) and the peyote cactus; in healing and divination rituals.

items.text: Ayahuasca: a DMT-containing plant boiled with another plant that activates it; healing and community ceremonies.
San Pedro in the Andes, and various plants in different regions; the common thread is ritual and spirituality.

sections.label: BRIDGE · 1957
sections.heading: A banker and a Mazatec healer brought the ancient tradition together with the modern West.

items.text: R. Gordon Wasson's mushroom ritual with María Sabina was published in Life magazine on 13 May 1957 — and it changed everything.

Why does it matter?

LSD was the first extraordinarily potent synthetic psychedelic
It offered a brand-new tool for studying the mind: "a lens for understanding the brain"
The de facto starting point of modern psychedelic science

lines: Swiss chemist; worked at the Sandoz pharmaceutical company
Synthesised LSD in 1938 while researching ergot derivatives
It sat on the shelf unnoticed for the first five years
He discovered its psychoactive effect by accident in 1943

items.text: ...an uninterrupted stream of fantastic pictures, extraordinary shapes with intense, kaleidoscopic play of colours...
"Bicycle Day": after absorbing the substance by accident, Hofmann cycled home; the first deliberate self-experiment thus entered history. Every 19 April is now marked as "Bicycle Day".

sections.label: SECTION 4 · 1947–1960
sections.heading: A "wonder drug" and a research boom

items.def: Sandoz distributed LSD to psychiatrists under the name "Delysid" — to be trialled as a tool in therapy.
1950s–60s: more than a thousand scientific publications, on conditions from alcoholism to anxiety.
Hofmann isolated and synthesised the active compound in María Sabina's mushroom — bringing it into the laboratory.
The CIA used LSD for mind control, at times on unwitting subjects and in unethical ways.

Timothy Leary tried the mushroom in Mexico in 1960
Started psilocybin research with Richard Alpert at Harvard
Over time the line between scientific rigour and advocacy blurred
1963: Leary and Alpert were dismissed from Harvard

lines: Conducted with 20 divinity students at Marsh Chapel
Half received psilocybin, half a placebo
Most of the psilocybin group reported a deep "mystical/religious" experience
Early evidence of the link between mystical experience and psychedelics

sections.label: SECTION 5 · COUNTERCULTURE
sections.heading: From the lab to the street

items.text: In the 1960s psychedelics spilled beyond the scientific world and became a symbol of the counterculture movement of the era.

items.def: Uncontrolled, widespread and unguided use; entirely outside the clinical frame.
Identified with the anti-war movement and youth rebellion; a perceived "threat" to those in power.
Exaggerated fear stories in the media; real risks and myths became mixed together.

items.text: LSD is progressively banned in the USA

items.def: Controlled Substances Act: the strictest category ("Schedule I")
UN Convention on Psychotropic Substances — the ban goes global
Clinical research effectively stops: the "dark period"
"Schedule I" = the class assumed to have no accepted medical use and a high potential for abuse — an assumption that also made research almost impossible.

sections.label: THE LESSON
sections.heading: In 20 years the same substance turned from "wonder drug" into "dangerous drug" — the molecule did not change, the context did.

items.text: This is a striking example of how much science can be influenced by social and political forces. We must learn to separate the scientific question from the cultural fear.

items.def: A quiet return, and today

lines: Rigorous research from the 1990s onwards
Johns Hopkins, Imperial, NYU, MAPS
Why now? — and the shadows of the renaissance

items.def: A non-profit organisation aiming to restart psychedelic research.
With strict ethical and regulatory approvals, small-scale human studies restarted.
Programmes at respected centres such as Johns Hopkins, Imperial College London and NYU.
An influential Johns Hopkins study showing psilocybin could produce lasting positive experiences under safe conditions.
Existing treatments are not enough for many patients with depression, PTSD and addiction.
A different mechanism and potentially faster, more lasting effect.
We can study the mechanisms with brain imaging and modern methods.
The social and regulatory climate has reopened to research.
Results are promising but limited; the "miracle cure" narrative is not realistic.
A fast-growing market; a risk of high cost and unequal access.
Vulnerability, suggestion and boundary violations raise serious ethical questions.
In most countries — including Türkiye — these substances are still illegal.

items.text: These shadows are the subject of the coming modules — it is essential to balance today's excitement with caution.

items.def: "Psychedelic" = mind-revealing. Even the choice of name gives away a stance.
Classic, entactogen, dissociative, atypical — different chemistry, effect and status.
Ritual use is very old; the ancestor of "set & setting" is there.
Science began in 1938, peaked in the 1960s, stopped in 1970.
Rigorous science since the 1990s; driven by unmet need — but with its shadows.

lines: Does the same substance being seen as "medicine" and as "drug" tell us more about science or about society?
What was gained and what was lost in moving from traditional/ritual use to modern medicine?

items.text: Common point: they all work via the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor (Section 2). Source, duration and intensity differ.

items.def: Natural, in certain mushrooms; converts to psilocin in the body. 4–6 hours. The most studied in clinical research; good safety profile in a controlled setting.
Laboratory-made; potent even in tiny amounts. 8–12 hours. Similar mechanism to psilocybin, but longer and more intense.
On its own very short (minutes) but intense. In the ayahuasca mixture its breakdown is prevented → an experience lasting hours.
In peyote and San Pedro cacti; among the oldest known classics. Long-lasting effect.

items.text: Module 2 · Substances and the Brain  ·  Section 1

items.def: Different from the classics: it does not radically alter perception. It mainly increases the release of serotonin (and dopamine, oxytocin) → intense emotional closeness, trust, empathy. This "emotional openness" makes it interesting for trauma work.
Ketamine — dissociative

items.text: A well-known drug used as an anaesthetic in medicine for decades. Works via an entirely different system (glutamate / NMDA). The only "psychedelic-like" substance used legally and approved for depression (Module 3).

sections.label: SECTION 1 · SUMMARY
sections.heading: Three different routes: 5-HT2A (classics), serotonin release (MDMA), glutamate/NMDA (ketamine).

items.text: These three routes mean three different experiences and three different clinical/legal statuses. Now let us open up the most researched route — the classics' 5-HT2A signature.

items.def:
What is serotonin, what does it do?
The 5-HT2A receptor and binding
Why it is not like a "reward/addiction" circuit
Module 2 · Substances and the Brain

sections.label: SEROTONIN
sections.heading: Serotonin is a signalling molecule with a role in mood, perception and cognition — one of the brain's "messengers".

items.text: Brain cells talk to each other with chemical signals. Serotonin is one of them; it is like a key that fits certain "locks" (receptors). The classic psychedelics fit one of those locks especially well — 5-HT2A.

items.def: The psychedelic molecule binds to the 5-HT2A receptor that serotonin normally binds to — often more strongly and differently than serotonin.

items.text: This binding starts an unusual pattern of activation in certain brain regions (especially the cortex).
The result: the signals carrying perception, thought and the sense of self are temporarily reorganised.
Key idea: the substance does not "add something new" to the brain; it puts an existing system (the serotonin circuit) into an unusual mode.
Module 2 · Substances and the Brain  ·  Section 2

items.def: Classic addictive drugs (opioids, cocaine) trigger the brain's dopamine-based "reward" circuit strongly and repeatedly. Classic psychedelics do not do this in the same way.
Tolerance to classic psychedelics develops very fast; taken on consecutive days the effect drops quickly. This does not "reward" continuous, compulsive use.

items.text: Psychological risks, difficult experiences and contraindications are real — we cover these in detail in Module 5.
Module 2 · Substances and the Brain  ·  Section 2

sections.label: SECTION 2 · SUMMARY
sections.heading: The classics' signature is a single receptor: 5-HT2A. This is a different door from the addiction circuit.

items.text: So what happens at the level of brain networks when this receptor is stimulated? The answer lies in one of the most talked-about concepts of recent years: the default mode network.

items.def:
What is the DMN, when is it active?
The self, the inner voice and habit patterns
How do psychedelics "loosen" this network?
Module 2 · Substances and the Brain

sections.label: THE DEFAULT MODE NETWORK
sections.heading: The DMN is the brain network most active when we are "doing nothing" — lost in thought, recalling the past, imagining the future.

items.text: It is associated with the "self", our "inner voice" and habitual thought patterns. It is the "default" mode that kicks in when your mind is not focused on a task — hence the name.

sections.label: SECTION 3 · FUNCTION
sections.heading: What is the DMN associated with?

items.def: The feeling of "I", and fixed stories and beliefs about ourselves (e.g. "I am this kind of person").
The continuously running inner speech; mental "chatter" and self-commentary.
Recalling the past and imagining the future — autobiographical thinking.
Habitual, automated pathways of thought — the brain's "familiar tracks".

items.text: A healthy DMN is necessary; but rigid, stuck-in-a-loop patterns may be at the core of some mental health problems (next slide).
Module 2 · Substances and the Brain  ·  Section 3

items.def:
Rigid, stuck thought patterns (the repetitions of depression, fixed negative beliefs) may soften during this loosening.
The brain finds the chance to form unusual new connections.
Some researchers describe this with the analogy of "temporarily resetting the brain".

lines: Brain imaging shows that classic psychedelics temporarily loosen the DMN's usual order.
The network's "tight" organisation dissolves; the usually dominant patterns weaken.
Subjectively, this is often described as "ego dissolution" / the melting of self-boundaries.

items.text: Module 2 · Substances and the Brain  ·  Section 3

sections.label: BRIDGE · DEPRESSION
sections.heading: If rigid thought patterns temporarily loosen, a person can look at old problems from a new place.

items.text: This is one of the main hypotheses trying to explain why psychedelics show promise in "stuck" states like depression and addiction. We cover the clinical evidence in Module 3. Now a short break.

items.def: ≈ 10 minutes  ·  Next: entropy and neuroplasticity

items.text: Module 2 · Substances and the Brain  ·  Break

items.def: The brain's "loosening" in two ideas

lines: Entropy / flexibility: increased cross-region communication
Neuroplasticity: the capacity to form new connections
The "window of change" and integration

items.def: Module 2 · Substances and the Brain
What happens IN THE MOMENT? The brain shows more communication between regions that do not usually talk to each other. It shifts into a more "fluid", less patterned state.
What REMAINS afterwards? The brain's capacity to form new connections and reorganise itself may be increased for a while — a "window of change".
One explains the "moment" of the experience, the other the "aftermath" — which is why they are complementary.

items.text: Module 2 · Substances and the Brain  ·  Section 4

items.def:
Communication increases between regions that usually do not talk.
The brain shifts into a more "fluid", less patterned state.
This flexibility is used to explain both the richness of the experience (new associations, imagery) and the therapeutic potential.

lines: Regions communicate along relatively fixed, familiar pathways.
This is efficient but also "patterned" and predictable.
Thought flows along familiar tracks.

items.text: Module 2 · Substances and the Brain  ·  Section 4

items.def: Neuroplasticity = the brain's capacity to form new connections (synapses) and reorganise itself.

items.text: Laboratory studies indicate that some psychedelics support the formation of synapses.
Even after the substance leaves the body, the brain may remain "open to change" for a while.
This is why therapeutic work is not only about the substance: the real work is the integration done while that window is open (Module 4).
Module 2 · Substances and the Brain  ·  Section 4

sections.label: SECTION 4 · SUMMARY
sections.heading: During the experience the brain is more flexible; after the experience it stays open to change for a while.

items.text: This "open window" idea explains why the therapeutic model is process-centred rather than drug-centred. But knowing what happens in the brain is not enough — what the person EXPERIENCES is also central. Next section: the subjective experience.

items.def: The other half of the mechanism

lines: Four commonly reported elements
Ego dissolution and the sense of meaning
The link between experience and recovery — and its debate

items.def: Module 2 · Substances and the Brain

sections.label: THE EXPERIENCE MATTERS
sections.heading: Beyond the scientific mechanisms, the experience people report itself seems to be central to the therapeutic effect.

items.text: This is a feature that sets psychedelics apart from most drugs: the effect may come not only from a chemical change but from the meaningful experience the person has.

items.def: Shifts in colours, sounds and the sense of time; intensified senses.
Long-suppressed emotions rising to the surface; crying, relief, release.
The temporary loosening of ordinary self-boundaries; feeling part of a larger whole.
Reporting a new perspective on one's life, relationships or problems.

items.text: These overlap with the mechanisms in Sections 3–4: DMN loosening ↔ ego dissolution; increased flexibility ↔ new insights.
Module 2 · Substances and the Brain  ·  Section 5

sections.label: MYSTICAL EXPERIENCE & RECOVERY
sections.heading: Research suggests there may be a link between intense insight/meaning ("mystical"-type) experiences and clinical recovery.

items.text: But note: the nature of this link is still debated and an active research topic. Correlation does not mean causation; whether the experience or the neurochemistry is decisive is an open question.

sections.label: DISCUSSION
sections.heading: Does recovery come from the chemistry, or from the meaningful experience? Is this a "drug", or an "experience"?

items.text: This distinction fundamentally changes how treatment is designed. Let us think briefly together — it is not a question with a single right answer.

items.def:
MDMA: softening the fear response
Ketamine: glutamate and rapid effect
Module 2 summary and the next step

lines: For some patients, talking about trauma is unbearably difficult because of the fear response.
When fear softens, the patient can approach the traumatic memory from a safer place.
This is why MDMA is central to trauma (PTSD) work (Module 3).
It does not radically alter perception like the classics.
It softens the fear and threat response; increases trust and emotional closeness.
It works by increasing the release of serotonin (and dopamine, oxytocin).

items.text: Module 2 · Substances and the Brain  ·  Section 6

sections.label: SECTION 6 · KETAMINE
sections.heading: Ketamine: a different system, rapid effect

items.def: Not serotonin; it works via an entirely different system (glutamate, the NMDA receptor).
It can show an antidepressant effect sometimes within hours — striking compared with the weeks of classic antidepressants.
The only "psychedelic-like" substance used legally/approved for depression (including esketamine).
It differs both in mechanism and legal status — which is why it sits in its own category.

items.text: We cover ketamine's clinical use and esketamine in detail in Module 3.
Module 2 · Substances and the Brain  ·  Section 6

items.def: Classics → 5-HT2A; MDMA → serotonin release; ketamine → glutamate/NMDA.
Temporary loosening of the "default mode network" can flex stuck thought patterns.
Neuroplasticity leaves a window open to change after the substance — the work is done in that window.
The subjective insight/meaning experience seems linked to clinical effect; but the mechanism is still debated.
Most explanations are at the hypothesis level; "not physically addictive" does not mean risk-free.

lines: If recovery comes from both chemistry and the meaningful experience, is this a "drug" or an "experience"? How does that distinction change treatment?
Are analogies like "resetting the brain" useful, or misleadingly oversimplified?
Subjective experience is hard to measure; how can science take something like "meaning" seriously and still remain rigorous?
How much evidence is needed to say we "know" a mechanism? Which of today's hypotheses do you trust most/least?

sections.label: THE UNMET NEED
sections.heading: Depression is one of the most common and most disabling conditions in the world — and a significant group of patients do not respond to existing drugs.

items.text: A picture that does not respond to two or more antidepressants is called "treatment-resistant depression". PTSD, too, is not always adequately treated by current methods. This gap is the focus of the research.

items.def: Patients who do not respond adequately to two or more antidepressants. A large group with a high sense of hopelessness. The main target of psilocybin research (Section 2).
Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)

items.text: Recalling and talking about trauma is often unbearably hard. Existing treatments do not work for everyone. The main target of MDMA research (Section 3).

items.def: Common point: neither are "easy" cases — which brings both high hope and the need to read the results with caution.

items.text: Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health  ·  Section 1

sections.label: SECTION 1 · BRIDGE
sections.heading: Research is not looking for "a pill for everyone"; it is looking for a new option for specific, hard conditions.

items.text: Now let us start with the area that has come furthest: psilocybin and treatment-resistant depression.

items.def: The area that has come furthest

lines: From early studies to Phase 3
COMP360: a first for a classic psychedelic
FDA acceleration and the "first approval" expectation

items.def: Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health

Most of these studies had small samples (few participants).
Therapeutic support always accompanied them — how much of the recovery is the substance, how much the support? (Section 6)
Early excitement tends to make results look more certain than they are.

lines: One or a few sessions were trialled in controlled, therapeutically supported conditions.
Some patients reported a rapid reduction in depressive symptoms lasting weeks.
These early findings excited the field and opened the way to larger trials.

items.text: Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health  ·  Section 2

sections.label: SECTION 2 · PHASE 3
sections.heading: COMP360: on the verge of a first

items.def: Compass Pathways' synthetic psilocybin (COMP360) met its primary endpoint in its first Phase 3 trial for treatment-resistant depression — the first positive Phase 3 result for a classic psychedelic in a psychiatric condition.
A second Phase 3 trial confirmed these results; the effect was reported to last weeks from one or two doses.
The company announced it aims to complete its FDA marketing application (NDA) by the end of 2026.

items.text: Source: Compass Pathways announcements; the situation may change — check official sources for current information.
Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health  ·  Section 2

sections.label: SECTION 2 · REGULATORY
sections.heading: FDA acceleration and the "first approval" expectation

items.def: In spring 2026 the USA granted accelerated/priority review status to psychedelic candidates — including psilocybin. This can shorten a review that normally takes months.

These developments strengthened the expectation that psilocybin could become the first FDA-approved classic psychedelic treatment under specific conditions. A decision is expected in late 2026 – early 2027.

items.text: Even with FDA approval, in the USA a separate DEA rescheduling is required; in Türkiye these substances remain illegal (Module 6).

sections.heading: Psilocybin–depression has the most mature evidence in the field; it is on the verge of a "first approval" but not yet across the finish line.

items.text: Now let us turn to a promising but more turbulent story: MDMA and PTSD — where we will see that the method, as much as the evidence, is put to the test.

items.def: A good result is not enough: the method is tested too

Phase 3 hope → the August 2024 FDA rejection
The lesson the field learned

items.def: Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health
For a trauma patient, the hardest part is often that recalling and talking about what happened is unbearably frightening.

items.text: MDMA softens the fear/threat response and creates trust and emotional openness (Module 2).
When fear softens enough, the patient can face the trauma therapeutically — from a safer place.
Key point: MDMA here is not a "pill that heals on its own"; it is thought of as a catalyst that makes psychotherapy possible.

sections.label: SECTION 3 · TURNING POINT
sections.heading: A promising result, an unexpected decision

items.def: Phase 3 trials of MDMA-assisted therapy gave positive results; the field expected it to be the first approved psychedelic treatment.
August 2024: FDA did not approve

items.text: The FDA did not approve the application as submitted (a "Complete Response Letter" to Lykos Therapeutics) and requested an additional Phase 3 trial.

items.def: This is one of the field's most discussed turning points: the gap between "a good result" and "approval" was seen exactly here.

items.text: Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health  ·  Section 3

items.def: The blinding problem
The effect is so obvious that it is very hard to hide whether a patient received the real substance or a placebo. This risks exaggerating the results.

items.text: A significant proportion of participants had used MDMA before; this can increase expectation and bias.
There were concerns that adverse events were under-reported at some sites.
These three concerns are not technical detail; they show why "proving" that a treatment truly works is hard (Section 6).
Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health  ·  Section 3

sections.label: SECTION 3 · THE LESSON
sections.heading: Promising results alone are not enough: methodological rigour, safety reporting and ethics are as decisive as the findings.

items.text: This decision did not slow the field, it matured it. (We cover the ethical dimension of the Lykos case in Module 5.) Now a short break.

items.def:
Existential distress in advanced illness
The dimension of meaning and acceptance
Psilocybin as a catalyst in addiction
Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health

lines: A single supported psilocybin session was reported to produce marked, long-lasting reductions in anxiety and depression.
A significant proportion of patients described relief in their attitude towards death.
Samples are small; the findings are promising but not conclusive.
Life-threatening illnesses (e.g. advanced cancer) can bring deep anxiety, depression and existential hopelessness.
This distress often does not respond well to standard treatments.

items.text: Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health  ·  Section 4

sections.label: MEANING AND ACCEPTANCE
sections.heading: These studies suggest psychedelics may be about not only "symptom reduction" but also the dimension of meaning and acceptance.

items.text: This is a promise that sets psychedelics apart from most psychiatric drugs — but it is also the dimension hardest to measure and to "prove" (Section 6).

sections.label: SECTION 4 · ADDICTION
sections.heading: Addiction: a banned substance, now a tool

items.def: Small studies offered promising (but not yet conclusive) results that psilocybin-assisted therapy may increase quit rates in smoking and alcohol addiction.
The catalyst idea

items.text: The logic here is to use the substance not as a means of pleasure but as a catalyst that helps the person gain insight into their own habits and motivation.

items.def: The irony: substances once banned as "drugs" are today being researched for treating addiction (recall the prohibition story of Module 1).

items.text: Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health  ·  Section 4

sections.label: SECTION 4 · SUMMARY
sections.heading: End of life and addiction show that psychedelics carry a promise "beyond symptom reduction" — but the evidence for that promise is still early.

items.text: Now let us flip it round: to the only example that is not in the research phase but has actually entered the clinic — ketamine.

items.def: The only example legal today

lines: Spravato: FDA-approved esketamine
The glutamate system and the speed advantage
Caution: durability and abuse

items.def: Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health
Esketamine, under the brand name Spravato, is a drug with FDA approval for treatment-resistant depression and major depression with suicidal ideation.
It works via the glutamate / NMDA system rather than serotonin (Module 2).
It can act sometimes within 24 hours — a significant speed advantage over the weeks-long effect of classic antidepressants.
Approved use is limited to supervised clinical settings; it is not free home use.

items.text: Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health  ·  Section 5

items.def: A durability problem
The effects may not be lasting; repeated administration may be needed. This creates difficulties for both cost and adherence.

items.text: Ketamine itself has abuse potential; this is why its use is limited to supervised settings.
Ketamine is a concrete example of the field's "legal but careful" balance: approval does not mean the problems are over.
Ketamine is the most concrete and most legal example in the field — and also the best example of the lesson "approval is a beginning, not an end".
Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health  ·  Section 5

sections.label: SECTION 5 · SUMMARY
sections.heading: Ketamine/esketamine is the only example legal and approved today — both the most concrete promise and the most realistic mirror of the field.

items.text: Now let us bring all these findings together and gain the real skill: how to read this evidence with caution?

items.def:
Why is blinding central?
Five points of caution
Module 3 summary and the next step
Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health

sections.label: SECTION 6 · BLINDING
sections.heading: The blinding problem: why does it matter so much?

items.def:
The effect is so obvious that the patient almost always knows they got the real substance.
This increases the expectation effect and can exaggerate the result.
The Good Friday experiment in Module 1 and the MDMA decision in Module 3 were both about exactly this problem.

lines: Neither the patient nor the researcher should know who got the real substance vs the placebo ("double-blind").
So one can tell whether recovery comes from the substance, not from expectation.

items.text: Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health  ·  Section 6

items.def: Many early studies had few participants. Phase 3 strengthens the picture, but the field is still young.
Because the effect is obvious, the placebo comparison weakens; results can be exaggerated.
How much of the recovery is the substance and how much the intense psychotherapeutic support — hard to separate.
The great excitement in the field can make positive results look more certain than they are.
These treatments are researched for specific patient groups and controlled conditions; not a general "miracle cure".

items.text: Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health  ·  Section 6

sections.label: HOPE AND CAUTION
sections.heading: Psychedelics offer real hope in some hard conditions; but science is still advancing, and a healthy scepticism towards exaggerated claims is the best approach.

items.text: Neither blanket rejection nor blind admiration: being a balanced reader who can tell the solid from the early.

items.def: The strongest evidence is in treatment-resistant depression (psilocybin) and PTSD (MDMA); both are on the edge of the regulatory process.
The FDA not approving the MDMA application in 2024 showed that methodological and ethical standards matter as much as the findings.
Ketamine/esketamine (Spravato) is the only example legal and approved today.
Small samples, the difficulty of blinding and expectation bias mean results must be read with balance.

items.text: Module 3 · Psychedelics and Mental Health  ·  Closing

lines: Why can it be so hard to "prove" that a treatment works — especially when the effect is felt so clearly?
Do you think the FDA not approving the MDMA application was good or bad for the field? Why?
How much of the recovery belongs to the substance and how much to the therapy — and why does knowing this matter?
When a headline says "psychedelics cure X", which five questions should you ask?

sections.label: WHAT WE WILL DO TODAY
sections.heading: By the end of this lesson you will understand why psychedelic recovery is possible not through the substance alone, but through a whole therapeutic process.

items.text: The aim is to see why the "take a pill and heal" narrative is misleading, and to grasp the role of set, setting, the three-phase model and integration.

items.def: Section 1 — "Not a drug, a process"
Section 2 — Set and setting
Section 3 — The three-phase model
Section 4 — The therapist's role and trust
Section 5 — Working with difficult experiences
Section 6 — Synthesis + closing
Module 4 · The Therapeutic Model  ·  Opening
From Module 3
Evidence was accumulating in psilocybin–depression and MDMA–PTSD — but always "under therapeutically supported conditions". Why?

items.text: How does recovery happen? Is it only the substance, or the process it sits within?
This is an information lesson; in Türkiye these substances are illegal; the model described is only for legal, clinical settings.
This module finally opens up what the phrases "therapeutic support", "controlled setting" and "integration" — repeated throughout the earlier modules — actually mean.

items.def:
What is effective is not the substance, but the process
Psychedelic-assisted therapy (PAT)
Substance = catalyst, therapy = the centre
Module 4 · The Therapeutic Model

sections.label: THE MOST MISUNDERSTOOD POINT
sections.heading: What is thought to be effective is not the substance alone; it is the structured therapeutic process the substance sits within.

items.text: Giving a patient psilocybin and leaving them alone in a room is NOT the model used in clinical studies. The substance is only one part of a frame made of preparation, support and the work done afterwards.

items.def: The field prefers the term "psychedelic-assisted therapy". The weight is on the therapy; the substance is a catalyst that assists it.
Substance = catalyst

items.text: A catalyst is something that makes a process happen but is not the process itself. The substance makes the therapeutic work possible and deep; but it is not what "does" the healing on its own.

items.def: Language matters (recall Module 1): not "psychedelic therapy" but "psychedelic-assisted therapy" — this small difference carries the essence of the whole model.

sections.label: SECTION 1 · BRIDGE
sections.heading: If the magic is not in the pill but in the process — then what is that process made of?

items.text: Let us start with two fundamental concepts that determine the quality of the experience: "set" and "setting".

items.def: The two concepts that shape the experience

lines: Set: mental preparation (the inner world)
Setting: the physical and social environment
The quality of the experience depends largely on these

items.def: Module 4 · The Therapeutic Model

sections.label: TWO FUNDAMENTAL CONCEPTS
sections.heading: The two most fundamental concepts of the field, carried from the 1960s to today: set and setting.

items.text: The same substance, the same dose — but a different inner world and a different environment produce a completely different experience. What determines the experience is largely not the substance, but these two contexts.

lines: The same substance leads to a completely different experience in an anxious, unprepared person.
And a completely different one in someone prepared and feeling safe.
This is why the preparation phase (Section 3) is the foundation of safety.
The inner world the person brings into the experience.
Mood, expectations, intention, past and their psychological state that day.
In short: "what are you bringing inside?"

items.text: How is it designed in the clinic?

lines: The environment is carefully designed: a calm, comfortable room.
Often an eye mask and carefully chosen music are used.
Trusted, trained people are present.
The physical and social environment in which the experience takes place.
The safety and quiet of the space, the atmosphere, whether trusted people are present.
In short: "what surrounds you outside?"

items.def: An anxious mind and an unsafe, chaotic environment can turn even a positive experience into a nightmare.
A prepared mind and a safe environment allow even difficult emotions to be processed safely.

items.text: This also explains why uncontrolled use is so risky.
When set and setting are not controlled, the same substance can turn into a traumatic and dangerous experience (Module 5).

sections.label: SECTION 2 · SUMMARY
sections.heading: The quality of the psychedelic experience depends largely not on the substance, but on set and setting.

items.text: So how are these two contexts built in practice? The answer is in the three-phase model used in clinical research.

items.def: Preparation · experience · integration

lines: Preparation: trust and intention
Dosing session: non-directive accompaniment
Integration: the most critical phase

items.def: Module 4 · The Therapeutic Model
Several meetings before the substance: building a trusting relationship, understanding the past and intention, explaining what to expect, discussing how to cope with difficult moments in advance.
The day the substance is administered in a supervised, supportive environment. One or two therapists stay with the patient for hours.
After the experience: working through together what it means and how to carry it into daily life.

items.text: The three phases are an inseparable whole; when one is missing, the process is incomplete.

items.def: Several meetings between patient and therapist(s). The aim: build a trusting relationship, understand the patient's past and intention, explain what to expect, and discuss in advance how to cope with possible difficult moments.
Experience session: non-directive accompaniment

items.text: The therapist does not direct or suggest the experience; they accompany the patient's own inner process in a safe space. The role is not "to guide" but "to keep safe".

items.def: "Non-directive" = not steering. The therapist does not bring content; the patient's own mind does (Module 1: "mind-revealing").

sections.label: SECTION 3 · INTEGRATION
sections.heading: Phase 3: integration — the most critical link

items.def:
"The neuroplasticity window": the brain stays open to change for a while.
Psychological work done while this window is open may be decisive for how lasting the effect is.
So integration overlaps exactly with the mechanism.

lines: After the experience, patient and therapist work through the meaning of what happened together.
Turning insights into lasting behaviour change happens in this phase.
Perhaps the most critical — and most neglected — phase.

sections.label: THE MAGIC IS NOT IN THE PILL
sections.heading: The magic is not in the pill, but in the process as a whole. Without integration, even a striking experience may bring no lasting benefit.

items.text: This is the essence of the whole module. After the break, we look at the relationship at the centre of this process — the therapist and trust.

items.def: ≈ 10 minutes  ·  Next: the therapist's role and trust
The relationship, at the centre of treatment

lines: Vulnerability and openness to suggestion
Why are trust and boundaries critical?
The task: to accompany, not to direct

items.def: Module 4 · The Therapeutic Model

sections.label: THE RELATIONSHIP AT THE CENTRE
sections.heading: In this model the therapeutic relationship is at the centre of treatment — because the patient, in a vulnerable and highly suggestible state, is in the same room with others for hours.

items.text: This is why trust, boundaries and professional ethics carry extraordinary importance. When the relationship is good the process is safe; when it is abused there is serious potential for harm.

items.def: The patient has the experience while most of their ordinary mental defences are temporarily down.
In this state a person is unusually open to suggestions, the environment and those around them.
The experience lasts for hours; throughout, the patient depends on the care of others.
Without trust, boundaries and ethics, this openness becomes a source of risk rather than protection.

items.text: This fragility fundamentally separates psychedelic therapy from an ordinary drug administration and raises the ethical bar very high.

items.def: Safe, non-judgemental accompaniment
The therapist's task is to accompany the patient's own inner process safely, without judgement and with respect — not to impose their own interpretations.

items.text: Physical and emotional boundaries are kept clear. When working with a vulnerable patient, boundary violations can cause serious harm.
The power imbalance is large; this is why professional ethics, supervision and accountability are essential (Module 5).
The therapist's role is not "the one who heals", but the one who holds the space in which healing can happen safely.

sections.label: SECTION 4 · SUMMARY
sections.heading: The relationship is both the most powerful tool of treatment and its most sensitive ethical point.

items.text: This frame of trust is tested most when things get "difficult". The next section: working with difficult experiences.

items.def: Is a "bad trip" necessarily bad?

lines: Difficult moments are not "going wrong"
In a safe frame they can be transformative
The keyword: safety

items.def: Module 4 · The Therapeutic Model

sections.label: DIFFICULT MOMENTS ARE NOT "WRONG"
sections.heading: Intense fear, anxiety and the surfacing of past pain are common — but these difficult moments are not necessarily something "going wrong".

items.text: In a therapeutic frame, difficult emotions that are met and processed safely can be the most transformative part of the process. Not a fault to avoid, but material to work with.

items.def: In a prepared environment, with supportive people and with integration afterwards, difficult experiences can be coped with healthily. The three-phase model makes exactly this possible.
In an uncontrolled setting

items.text: The same difficult experience, without preparation, support and integration, can be traumatic and dangerous. The difference is not in the substance, but in the frame.

items.def: The same experience can produce two opposite outcomes in two different frames — the most striking example of the module's "the process is decisive" message.

sections.label: SECTION 5 · SUMMARY
sections.heading: Difficult experiences are neither necessarily bad nor to be romanticised — what is decisive is the frame in which they are processed.

items.text: Now let us bring all the pieces together and see what this model teaches us beyond psychedelics.

items.def:
The whole process in one picture
What does this model say for psychotherapy?
Module 4 summary and the next step
Module 4 · The Therapeutic Model

sections.label: SECTION 6 · SYNTHESIS
sections.heading: The whole process in one picture

items.def: = Therapeutic recovery

items.text: No single component is enough on its own; recovery emerges from this whole. The substance is only one factor — but on its own it does nothing.

sections.label: A SURPRISING CONCLUSION
sections.heading: If success depends largely on "environment" and "relationship", might this teach us something about non-psychedelic psychotherapies too?

items.text: Set, setting, trust and integration are actually the components of every good therapeutic process. Psychedelics perhaps only make them more visible and more intense.

items.def: What is effective is the whole process of substance + preparation + support + integration.
Mental preparation and the environment largely determine the quality of the experience.
Preparation, the experience session and integration work together; integration is the most neglected but most critical phase.
Difficult experiences are not necessarily negative; but they can only be processed within a safe, supported, relationship-based frame.

lines: If the success of a treatment depends largely on "environment" and "relationship", what does this teach us about non-psychedelic psychotherapies?
Why might integration be so often neglected — and is this connected to our expectation of a "quick fix"?
What is the difference between "non-directive" accompaniment and "leaving the patient alone"?
What does the fact that the same difficult experience can be transformative in one place and traumatic in another imply for drug policy?

items.text: We have seen the power of the process — but what about its shadows? Physical and psychological risks, contraindications, harm reduction, and the field's most sensitive point: ethics.

sections.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to weigh the real risks of psychedelics, who they are unsuitable for, and the field's ethical problems in a balanced way.

items.text: The aim is neither "dangerous drug" panic nor "risk-free miracle" fantasy; it is a view that recognises the real risks, knows the contraindications and takes the ethical questions seriously.

From Module 4
We saw the healing power of the process (set, setting, relationship, integration). But every powerful thing has its shadows.

items.text: What are the risks, who are they unsuitable for, and are "it works" and "it is done right" the same thing?
This lesson does NOT recommend personal use; in Türkiye these substances are illegal. The aim is academic awareness.
The "vulnerability" of Module 4 and the "FDA rejection" of Module 3 will be fully opened up in this module — especially in the ethics section.
Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics  ·  Opening
A balanced view and physical risks

items.def:
Both extremes are misleading
The safety margin of the classics — but not risk-free
The physical risks of MDMA and uncontrolled settings
Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics

sections.label: NEITHER TOO LITTLE NOR TOO MUCH
sections.heading: Both extremes are misleading: treating these as "entirely dangerous drugs" and seeing them as "risk-free miracle cures".

items.text: The true picture is in the middle: under controlled conditions some substances have a relatively good safety profile, but real and serious risks exist — especially in uncontrolled use.

items.def:
Blood pressure and heart rate can rise — a risk for those with cardiovascular problems.
Nausea, vomiting (especially with ayahuasca) and loss of coordination are common.
Impaired judgement increases the risk of accidents and injury.

lines: Psilocybin, LSD: a relatively wide safety margin regarding lethal dose compared with many common substances.
They are not physically addictive in the classic sense.

items.text: Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics  ·  Section 1

items.def: Especially in uncontrolled settings: a dangerous rise in body temperature (hyperthermia), disruption of salt-water balance, and serious strain on the heart. These can be life-threatening.

items.text: Most of these risks multiply in hot, crowded settings where the dose and content are unknown. The clinical model is built precisely to control these variables (Section 4).
The content of "MDMA" sold on the street is often unknown — which makes the dose and interactions entirely unpredictable.
Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics  ·  Section 1

sections.label: SECTION 1 · SUMMARY
sections.heading: Physical risks are real, but most multiply with uncontrolled use and unknown content/dose.

items.text: Even so, with the classic psychedelics the more important risks are not physical — they are psychological. The next section focuses there.

items.def: The more important area

lines: Intense fear and panic
Prolonged negative effects
HPPD and the risk of triggering psychosis

items.def: Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics

sections.label: THE REAL RISKS ARE PSYCHOLOGICAL
sections.heading: With classic psychedelics the more important risks are in the psychological domain — and depend largely on context (set and setting).

items.text: This shows once again why Module 4 is so important: in a bad context, psychological risk rises sharply.

items.def: A difficult experience ("bad trip") in an uncontrolled setting can be traumatic. Without a safe frame, it can become unbearable in the moment (Module 4).
Prolonged negative effects

items.text: In some people, anxiety, restlessness or distress lasting days to weeks can appear after the experience. It may not all be over when the experience ends.

items.def: These two risks show that "the experience itself is short but its effects can persist" — which is another reason integration (Module 4) matters.

items.text: Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics  ·  Section 2

sections.label: SECTION 2 · RISK 3–4
sections.heading: HPPD and the risk of triggering psychosis

items.def: Rare but real: in some people, visual perception disturbances (e.g. persistent "trails", hallucination-like images) that continue after the substance's effect has passed have been reported.
Risk of triggering psychosis

items.text: One of the most serious concerns. In predisposed people it can trigger a psychotic process. This is the basis for the contraindications in the next section.

items.def: These two risks raise directly the question "who is it unsuitable for?" — the subject of the next section.

items.text: Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics  ·  Section 2

sections.label: SECTION 2 · SUMMARY
sections.heading: Psychological risks — fear, prolonged effects, HPPD, triggering psychosis — rise sharply with uncontrolled use.

items.text: And for some people the risk is so high that even clinical studies exclude them. Who? The next section.

items.def:
A history of psychosis / bipolar disorder
Certain cardiovascular conditions
Drug interactions: SSRIs, MAOIs
Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics
Personal or a strong family history. Classic psychedelics can trigger a psychotic or manic episode — the most important contraindication.
A rise in blood pressure and heart rate can endanger existing cardiovascular problems.
Excluded because safety data are insufficient or the risk is high.

items.text: These groups are not "arbitrary"; each rests on a real, documented basis of risk.
Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics  ·  Section 3

items.def: Some combinations can be fatal. For example, MAOI-class antidepressants taken together with MDMA can be life-threatening.
Some antidepressants (SSRIs) can alter the effect of psychedelics or produce dangerous interactions. This is why drug history is carefully assessed in the clinic.
Here is the most concrete danger of uncontrolled use:

items.text: A person may not know their own risk factors or the interactions of the drugs they take; without medical supervision these interactions can be fatal.
Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics  ·  Section 3

sections.label: WHY IS UNCONTROLLED USE DANGEROUS?
sections.heading: Because a person may not know their own risk factors — and without medical screening, a safe environment and supervision, risks grow unpredictably.

items.text: The clinical model is built precisely to remove these risk factors. After the break we cover this through the concept of "harm reduction".

items.def: ≈ 10 minutes  ·  Next: harm reduction and ethics

items.text: Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics  ·  Break

items.def: Targeting the source of harm

lines: What is harm reduction?
The real sources of risk
How does the clinical model remove them?

items.def: Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics

sections.label: WHAT IS HARM REDUCTION?
sections.heading: "Harm reduction" is a public-health approach that aims to minimise harm in situations where use is taking place.

items.text: IMPORTANT: The scope of this programme is NOT to recommend personal use, and in Türkiye these substances are illegal. We cover these principles only academically, to understand the logic of the risks.

sections.label: SECTION 4 · SOURCES
sections.heading: Where do the risks come from?

items.def: Not knowing the substance, the dose and one's own risk factors.
Substances of uncertain content and unpredictable doses.
An unsafe, chaotic or unsupported set and setting (Module 4).
Failing to notice contraindications and drug interactions (Section 3).

items.text: Note: none of these four sources means "the substance itself is inevitably harmful" — they are all about context.
Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics  ·  Section 4

sections.label: WHY DOES THE CLINICAL MODEL MATTER?
sections.heading: The clinical model is built precisely to remove these risk factors: medical screening, a safe environment, preparation and supervision.

items.text: So the structured process described in Module 4 is at the same time the most powerful safety mechanism. Now we move to the field's most sensitive point: ethics.
Ethics: the field's most sensitive point

items.def:
Openness to suggestion
Boundary violations and abuse
The Lykos case, blinding and expectation
Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics

sections.label: VULNERABILITY → ETHICAL RISK
sections.heading: Psychedelic therapy puts the patient in an extraordinarily vulnerable and suggestible state — and this creates serious ethical risks.

items.text: In Module 4 we saw this vulnerability as an "opportunity for healing". The same vulnerability, when abused, is a source of serious harm. This section works through those risks one by one.

items.def: Why is it so serious?

lines: The patient is exposed to these suggestions while most of their critical defences are down.
This is why the non-directive approach (Module 4) is not just a preference but an ethical necessity.
The therapist's task is not to impose interpretations, but to hold a safe space.
During the experience the patient can be excessively influenced by the therapist's words, beliefs and expectations.
The therapist "instilling" their own world-view (religious, philosophical, personal) into the patient is a real risk.

items.text: Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics  ·  Section 5
In this state where the patient is vulnerable, physical contact, privacy and professional boundaries become extraordinarily critical.

items.def: Serious boundary-violation and abuse cases in the field's past have clearly shown why strict ethical protocols and supervision are essential.
The power imbalance is very large: this is why clear boundaries, recording, supervision and accountability are not negotiable.

items.text: Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics  ·  Section 5

sections.label: SECTION 5 · ETHICAL RISK 3–4
sections.heading: The Lykos case, blinding and expectation

items.def: Behind the FDA rejection mentioned in Module 3 were also ethical violations in a clinical trial and their under-reporting. It showed why the attitude "if the result is good, the method does not matter" is unacceptable.
"Blinding" and expectation

items.text: The strong beliefs of both patients and researchers towards these substances make scientific objectivity harder (the blinding problem of Module 3).

items.def: The shared lesson: in this field, "good intentions" and "good results" do not substitute for rigorous method and ethics.

items.text: Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics  ·  Section 5

sections.label: SECTION 5 · THE LESSON
sections.heading: "It works" and "it is done right" are not the same thing — and the maturity of a field is measured by its ability to tell them apart.

items.text: Ethics is not an add-on ornament; it is the precondition of working with a vulnerable person. In the final section we look at a broader problem — commercialisation and justice.

items.def:
Cost and unequal access
Cultural appropriation
Module 5 summary and the next step
Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics
If treatments are approved they may be very expensive; this could create an inequality where only the wealthy can access them.

items.text: Commercialising the plants and knowledge that indigenous peoples have used for centuries raises questions of cultural appropriation and justice (Module 1).
Unrealistic expectations, exaggerated promises and unregulated clinics are a risk.
Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics  ·  Section 6

items.def: The safety profile is relatively good under controlled conditions; but risks — especially psychological and in uncontrolled use — are real.
A history of psychosis/bipolar and some drug interactions (especially MAOIs) are serious, real risks.
Openness to suggestion, boundary violations and the power imbalance require strict protocols and supervision.
Commercialisation, unequal access and cultural justice are open problems in the field.

items.text: Module 5 · Risks, Safety and Ethics  ·  Closing

lines: Even if a treatment truly works, if the way it is delivered is unethical, should society trust that treatment?
Why is the difference between "it works" and "it is done right" so important?
Considering the contraindications and interactions, why can uncontrolled use not be seen as merely "a personal choice"?
If commercialisation is inevitable, what can be done to protect equity of access and cultural justice?

sections.label: WHY A COMPLEX PICTURE?
sections.heading: The legal status of psychedelics changes both from country to country and rapidly over time.

items.text: In most countries these substances are still in the strictest banned category. But as scientific findings accumulate, some countries have begun to open narrow doors to medical/research use. The picture below is as of July 2026 and can change quickly.
Module 6 · Legal Status, the Future and Responsible Engagement

sections.label: SECTION 1 · USA
sections.heading: The USA: federal ban, but movement

items.text: At the federal level classic psychedelics are still in "Schedule I" (the strictest) category. But there was significant movement in 2024–2026:

items.def: Already FDA-approved and in clinical use (Spravato).
In August 2024 the FDA did not approve the application and requested an additional trial.
COMP360 achieved positive Phase 3 results in 2025 and 2026; the company targets a submission by the end of 2026.

items.text: Module 6 · Legal Status, the Future and Responsible Engagement  ·  Section 1

items.def: In April 2026 a presidential order directed federal agencies to accelerate the research and approval of psychedelic treatments. The FDA granted accelerated review status to psilocybin and some MDMA-like compounds.
State level: Oregon and Colorado

items.text: Independently of the federal ban, Oregon (Measure 109) and Colorado (Natural Medicine Health Act) set up supervised, adult psilocybin service/healing centres — not by prescription, but supervised and on-site.

items.def: Federal and state levels can conflict: a substance may be used under supervision in a state while still federally illegal.

items.text: Module 6 · Legal Status, the Future and Responsible Engagement  ·  Section 1

sections.label: SECTION 1 · SUMMARY
sections.heading: The USA appears to be on the verge of the first FDA-approved classic psychedelic treatment — but this is not yet settled.

items.text: Now let us look at the country that has already moved to prescription use, setting a world first: Australia.

items.def: A first and a mixed picture

lines: Australia: a world first in 2023
Real-world practice
Europe: a cautious and variable opening

items.def: Module 6 · Legal Status, the Future and Responsible Engagement
In 2023 Australia moved MDMA and psilocybin out of the strictest category; it took effect on 1 July 2023. Authorised psychiatrists can prescribe them under specific conditions.

items.text: MDMA only for PTSD, psilocybin only for treatment-resistant depression — and only through psychiatrists who have obtained special authorisation.

items.def: This is not "over-the-counter sale"; it is a narrow medical door under strict authorisation and supervision.

items.text: Module 6 · Legal Status, the Future and Responsible Engagement  ·  Section 2

items.def: From early 2024 patients began receiving treatment under this scheme; patient numbers rose gradually from mid-2025. In 2026 more flexible delivery rules came in.
Valuable but contested

items.text: Australia offers a valuable — and contested — real-world example of clinical practice: live debates continue over cost, access and standards.
Why does it matter? Other countries and regulators are learning from Australia's experience — both its successes and its problems.
Module 6 · Legal Status, the Future and Responsible Engagement  ·  Section 2

items.def: Most countries maintain a strict ban; some have research studies and limited windows of use.
Some countries allow ketamine clinics and clinical research.
The European Medicines Agency is watching developments closely; the general trend is a cautious "medicalisation" opening.

items.text: The pace varies greatly from country to country — Europe should not be thought of as a single picture.

sections.heading: The general trend is a cautious "medicalisation" opening — but the pace and form vary greatly from country to country.

sections.label: TÜRKİYE: THE CLEAR SITUATION
sections.heading: In Türkiye, psilocybin, LSD, MDMA and similar psychedelic substances are illegal.

items.text: Under the Turkish Penal Code these substances are classified as "narcotic and stimulant substances". Even personal use carries serious sanctions, including imprisonment.
Module 6 · Legal Status, the Future and Responsible Engagement

items.def: TPC article 191 makes using, purchasing, receiving or possessing a narcotic/stimulant substance a criminal offence.
Manufacture and trafficking

items.text: TPC article 188 prohibits the manufacture, import/export and trafficking of these substances with far heavier penalties. As LSD and MDMA are synthetic, an increased penalty may apply.

items.def: A firm boundary:

items.text: In Türkiye any personal experiment, sourcing or use of these substances is strictly illegal, and this programme does not recommend it in any way.
Module 6 · Legal Status, the Future and Responsible Engagement  ·  Section 3

sections.label: SECTION 3 · IN PRACTICE
sections.heading: Ketamine and the meaning of this field in Türkiye

items.def: As a medicine, ketamine may be used only under a doctor's supervision and for licensed indications. Sourcing or using it without prescription is illegal.
How is this field meaningful?

items.text: For participants in Türkiye, this field is meaningful only as a scientific, academic and professional interest — following research and regulation abroad. Not as practical application.

items.def: In other words: curiosity and academic interest are entirely legitimate; but this interest does not legitimise any unlawful behaviour.

lines: Medicalisation: a supervised clinical model
Access, cost and scientific maturation
The risk of backlash: history can repeat

items.def: Module 6 · Legal Status, the Future and Responsible Engagement

Psilocybin and perhaps MDMA-like compounds may be approved as strictly supervised clinical treatments in a few countries. A model that is "administered in the clinic, under supervision", not "bought at the pharmacy".
Access and cost

items.text: Even if approval comes, high cost and the need for expert therapists may limit how widespread these treatments become — unequal access is a real risk (Module 5).

items.def: An important point: "approval" and "everyone being able to access" are very different things; the latter can be much slower and more unequal.

items.text: Module 6 · Legal Status, the Future and Responsible Engagement  ·  Section 4

sections.label: SECTION 4 · SCENARIO 3–4
sections.heading: Maturation and the risk of backlash

items.def: Larger, more rigorous trials will clarify which patient benefits from what. Hope may increasingly rest on more solid evidence.
The risk of backlash

items.text: A safety scandal, poor practice or unmet exaggerated expectations could set the field back again. History shows this is possible (the 1960s).

items.def: Recall the lesson of Module 1: in 20 years the same substance turned from "wonder drug" into "dangerous drug". Context can change everything.

items.text: Module 6 · Legal Status, the Future and Responsible Engagement  ·  Section 4

sections.label: SECTION 4 · SUMMARY
sections.heading: The future is most likely towards strictly supervised medicalisation — but the risk of backlash is real and historical.

items.text: In the face of this uncertainty, what can an individual do? Before the closing, let us cover the most practical question: the responsible path.

sections.label: MUCH IS POSSIBLE WITHIN BOUNDS
sections.heading: A person interested in this field can do a great deal while staying within legal and ethical bounds.

items.text: Being interested and acting unlawfully are not the same thing. Curiosity is legitimate; there are concrete ways to channel it responsibly.

sections.label: SECTION 5 · PATHS 1–3
sections.heading: The responsible path: the first three steps

items.def: Respect for the law
Following reliable academic sources; being able to tell exaggerated claims from serious research (the "reading the evidence" skill of Module 3).

items.text: Knowing that these substances are illegal in Türkiye and abiding by it. Interest does not legitimise unlawful behaviour.
For mental-health professionals: deepening knowledge in neuroscience, psychotherapy and research methods.
Module 6 · Legal Status, the Future and Responsible Engagement  ·  Section 5

sections.label: SECTION 5 · PATHS 4–5
sections.heading: The responsible path: the last two steps

items.def: Without getting swept up in the field's excitement, being able to see the potential, the risks and the ethical problems together — the aim of this whole programme.
In distress: professional support

items.text: If there is a personal mental-health difficulty, turning to an authorised mental-health professional rather than to unsupervised substances. This is the most important practical message.

items.def: The fifth point is critical: this lesson is not a solution, but a framework. In a real difficulty, the right address is an authorised professional.

sections.label: THE AIM OF THE PROGRAMME
sections.heading: The aim was to turn you into neither an advocate nor a sceptic — but to give you a framework to read this field in an informed, balanced and critical way.

items.text: The place of psychedelics in mental health is one of the most interesting and most contested stories of modern science: they may carry real potential; they are also surrounded by serious risks, unresolved ethical questions and important legal limits.
Module 6 · Legal Status, the Future and Responsible Engagement

items.def: Ketamine approved; psilocybin on the verge of approval; MDMA delayed in the process; Australia opened to prescription use.
These substances are illegal in Türkiye (TPC 188/191); the programme is for academic/information purposes only.
Towards strictly supervised medicalisation; but the risk of backlash is also real.
Scientific literacy, respect for the law, a critical and ethical view.

items.text: Module 6 · Legal Status, the Future and Responsible Engagement  ·  Closing
When a topic carries both great hope and serious risk, how should we as a society strike the balance between "hasty approval" and "excessive caution"?

lines: This question is not only about psychedelics — it applies to new drugs, technologies and medical innovations too.
The 1960s of Module 1 (over-excitement → harsh ban) and the FDA rigour of Module 3 show the two ends of this balance.
It is not a question with a single right answer; but it is worth reflecting on as an informed citizen and professional.
